## Setup {.unnumbered}

We will need to load the following packages before proceeding:

```{webr}
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(modelr)
library(quantreg)
```

## DoorDash ETAs — Thinking Like the ETA Team! {.unnumbered}

![Copyright © 2026 DoorDash, Inc.](img/doordash-logo.png){width=70%}

Imagine you have just joined the **DoorDash ETA (Estimated Time of Arrival) team** as a Data Scientist. Your manager does not care about “*average delivery time*” in the abstract; they care about **customer promises**:

- *“Most orders should arrive around ___ minutes.”*  
- *“But we should warn customers that it could take as long as ___ minutes.”*  
- *“And we need to understand how staffing and congestion shift those numbers.”*

This warmup is about learning the tool that matches that reality: **Quantile regression**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Important Key Mindset Shift
In this setting, focusing only on the Ordinary Least-squares (OLS) conditional mean $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid X)$ is often *not the right target*. Let us suppose that DoorDash lives and dies by **the median** (typical experience), **upper quantiles** (late orders, disappointed customers), and **lower quantiles** (early orders and possibly happier customers).

:::

## About the Dataset {.unnumbered}

The **DoorDash ETA** dataset contains historical delivery records from early 2015, where each observation corresponds to a single food delivery order. The response of interest is the total delivery duration, defined as the time between when an order is placed (`created_at`) and when it is delivered (`actual_delivery_time`). 

The dataset includes a mix of order characteristics, marketplace conditions at order time (e.g., number of active and busy dashers nearby), and predictions from internal models (e.g., estimated driving time). Because delivery times are typically right-skewed and heterogeneous, this dataset is well-suited for Quantile regression, which allows us to model different parts of the conditional distribution of delivery time rather than just the mean. You can find the dataset in [**this Kaggle website**](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/dharun4772/doordash-eta-prediction?resource=download). **Suppose this dataset is representative enough for a given city of interest**.

## Setup: Load the Dataset {.unnumbered}

The raw dataset `doordash.csv` includes timestamps for when an order is placed and when it is delivered, plus features describing **market conditions** and **order/store characteristics**. We have 12969 raw data points.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
doordash_raw <- read_csv("datasets/doordash.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(doordash_raw)
```

## Data Wrangling: Define the response we actually model! {.unnumbered}

In the raw data `doordash_raw`, columns `created_at` and `actual_delivery_time` are timestamps. For modelling and interpretation, we will convert these into an **actual delivery duration in minutes**. Note that we will overwrite `actual_delivery_time` to be the duration in min (suppose DoorDash people often casually call this “*actual delivery time*” anyway). The original delivery timestamp will be stored as `actual_delivery_timestamp`. The below chunk of code results in a data frame of $n = 12700$ rows, which is enough data.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# We select the necessary columns for our inquiries.
# Then, we create actual_delivery_time using {lubridate} functions.
training_doordash <- doordash_raw |>
  dplyr::select(
    created_at,
    actual_delivery_time,
    total_onshift_dashers,
    total_busy_dashers,
    store_primary_category
  ) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(
    created_at = ymd_hms(created_at, tz = "UTC"),
    actual_delivery_timestamp = ymd_hms(actual_delivery_time, tz = "UTC"),
    actual_delivery_time = as.numeric(difftime(actual_delivery_timestamp,
      created_at,
      units = "mins"
    ))
  ) |>
  drop_na() # Dropping final rows with NAs due to incorrect raw timestamp records.
```

Let us now check summary of `actual_delivery_time`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
summary(training_doordash$actual_delivery_time)
```

Now, let us plot the histogram of `actual_delivery_time` via `training_doordash`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
hist_actual_delivery_time <- ggplot(
  training_doordash,
  aes(x = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 60,
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "black",
    linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(actual_delivery_time)),
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.5, color = "red"
  ) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = median(actual_delivery_time)),
    linetype = "solid", linewidth = 0.5, color = "red"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Actual Delivery Time (min)",
    y = "Number of Orders",
    title = "Histogram of DoorDash Actual Delivery Times",
    subtitle = "Solid vertical line = median, dashed vertical line = mean"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 22),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 21)
  )
hist_actual_delivery_time
```

**Q1.1.1.**	Based on the above descriptive statistics and histogram, which is the better “*typical ETA*” and why?

## First Statistical Inquiry: “What’s ‘typical’ delivery time, and how do staffing plus congestion move it?” {.unnumbered}

Your manager asks:

> “*I don’t want the average — I want typical delivery time. Use staffing within 10 miles (`total_onshift_dashers`, $X_1$) and congestion (`total_busy_dashers`, $X_2$) to explain what shifts that typical time.*”

We will compare:

-	**OLS**: models the conditional mean $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid X_1, X_2)$.
- **Parametric median Quantile regression ($\tau = 0.5$):** models the conditional median $Q_{Y \mid X_1, X_2}(\tau = 0.5 \mid X_1, X_2)$.

The exact regressor descriptions are the following:

- `total_onshift_dashers`: Number of available dashers who are within 10 miles of the store at the time of order creation.
- `total_busy_dashers`: Subset of the above `total_onshift_dashers` who are currently working on an order.

## Q1.6. Graphical comparison: OLS Fitted Line versus Parametric Median Quantile Fitted Line {.unnumbered}

To make a clean comparison against one regressor at a time between OLS and parametric median Quantile regression, we will:

- Vary one (either `total_onshift_dashers` or `total_busy_dashers`) across its range.
- Hold the other regressor fixed at its median.
- Plot predicted mean (OLS) versus predicted median ($\tau=0.5$).

**Plot A: Vary on-shift dashers and hold busy dashers fixed**

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
grid_onshift <- tibble(
  total_onshift_dashers = seq(
    min(training_doordash$total_onshift_dashers),
    max(training_doordash$total_onshift_dashers),
    length.out = 200
  ),
  total_busy_dashers = median(training_doordash$total_busy_dashers)
) |>
  mutate(
    pred_OLS = predict(ETA_OLS, newdata = cur_data()),
    pred_qr_50 = predict(ETA_param_qr_50, newdata = cur_data())
  )

plot_delivery_time_vs_onshift <- ggplot(
  training_doordash,
  aes(x = total_onshift_dashers, y = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, color = "darkblue") +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_onshift, aes(y = pred_OLS),
    linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed", color = "chocolate"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_onshift, aes(y = pred_qr_50),
    linewidth = 0.6, color = "chocolate"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Total On-shift Dashers (within 10 miles)",
    y = "Actual Delivery Time (min)",
    title = "Mean (OLS, dashed) versus Parametric Median (0.5-quantile, solid)",
    subtitle = "Total busy dashers held constant at its median"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 19, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 18)
  )
plot_delivery_time_vs_onshift
```

**Plot B: Vary busy dashers, hold on-shift dashers fixed**

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
grid_busy <- tibble(
  total_busy_dashers = seq(
    min(training_doordash$total_busy_dashers),
    max(training_doordash$total_busy_dashers),
    length.out = 200
  ),
  total_onshift_dashers = median(training_doordash$total_onshift_dashers)
) |>
  mutate(
    pred_OLS = predict(ETA_OLS, newdata = cur_data()),
    pred_qr_50 = predict(ETA_param_qr_50, newdata = cur_data())
  )

plot_delivery_time_vs_busy <- ggplot(
  training_doordash,
  aes(x = total_busy_dashers, y = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, color = "darkgreen") +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_busy, aes(y = pred_OLS),
    linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed", color = "chocolate"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_busy, aes(y = pred_qr_50),
    linewidth = 0.6, color = "chocolate"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Total Busy Dashers",
    y = "Actual Delivery Time (min)",
    title = "Mean (OLS, dashed) versus Parametric Median (0.5-quantile, solid)",
    subtitle = "Total on-shift dashers held constant at its median"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 19, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 18)
  )
plot_delivery_time_vs_busy
```

### What the Manager Wants! {.unnumbered}

The manager wants to assess whether there is a statistical association between the
$\tau = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9$ conditional quantiles of `actual_delivery_time` versus:

- `total_onshift_dashers`: Number of available dashers who are within 10 miles of the store at the time of order creation.
- `total_busy_dashers`: Subset of the above `total_onshift_dashers` who are currently working on an order.
- `store_primary_category`: Cuisine category of the restaurant, e.g., Italian, Mexican, Chinese, Indian, etc.

... and by how much, if significant.

::: {.callout-important}
## Important
Quantile regression will let us answer it across the distribution of actual delivery times. Moreover, there will be three fitted parametric Quantile regression models: $\tau = 0.1$ (say, early deliveries, and possibly, happier customers), $\tau = 0.5$ (say, typical experience), and $\tau = 0.9$ (say, late orders with possible disappointed customers).
:::

### Data Wrangling {.unnumbered}

`store_primary_category` has many categories, which can be noisy for a warmup exercise. Thus, we will keep the most common categories and drop the rest into a factor level called "`Other`". This will result in a factor-type column `store_primary_category` with nine categories only.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
training_doordash_2 <- training_doordash |>
  mutate(
    store_primary_category = fct_lump_n(store_primary_category,
      n = 8, other_level = "Other"
    )
  )
count(training_doordash_2, store_primary_category, sort = TRUE)
```

### Q1.7. Exploratory Data Analysis: Quantile thinking! {.unnumbered}

Before we fit any model, we want to **see** how delivery times behave under different marketplace conditions and order characteristics. But here is the key DoorDash insight:

- The **mean** can be a misleading summary because late deliveries create a long right tail.
- What we really care about operationally is how regressors move:

  + **early deliveries** ($\tau = 0.1$).
  + **typical deliveries** (the median, $\tau = 0.5$).
  + **slow deliveries** ($\tau = 0.9$).

So, in this exploratory data analysis (EDA), we will look at scatterplots and category comparisons, but instead of drawing a “*best-fit mean line*,” we will overlay **fitted parametric Quantile regression lines** for $\tau = 0.1, 0.5, 0.9$. Think of these three lines as a first-pass picture of the ETA system:

- The $\tau = 0.1$ fitted line is an **early-delivery curve** (ideal to have happier customers).
- The $\tau = 0.5$ fitted line is a **typical ETA curve** (robust to late outliers).
- The $\tau = 0.9$ fitted line is a **late-delivery risk curve** (what customers complain about).
- The gap between $\tau = 0.1$ and $\tau = 0.9$ fitted lines is a preview of an **ETA interval**.

With that mindset, let us visualize how staffing (`total_onshift_dashers`) and congestion (`total_busy_dashers`) relate to the lower, middle, and upper parts of delivery time. We will illustrate these fitted Quantile regression lines per regressor with respect to `actual_delivery_time` (**just for EDA purposes**, a more complete model fitting for inferential purposes will be explained later on).

::: {.callout-important}
## Important
The usual `geom_quantile(y ~ x)` fits *marginal* quantile curves that only condition on the $x$-axis variable. Here, we would prefer *conditional* quantile curves from a model that takes into account both `total_onshift_dashers` and `total_busy_dashers`. So, we fit parametric Quantile regressions using both regressors, then plot predictions while varying one regressor and holding the other fixed (at its median). This makes the visual comparison meaningful.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
# 1) Fit parametric Quantile regressions just for EDA.
qr10 <- rq(actual_delivery_time ~ total_onshift_dashers + total_busy_dashers,
  tau = 0.1, data = training_doordash_2
)
qr50 <- rq(actual_delivery_time ~ total_onshift_dashers + total_busy_dashers,
  tau = 0.5, data = training_doordash_2
)
qr90 <- rq(actual_delivery_time ~ total_onshift_dashers + total_busy_dashers,
  tau = 0.9, data = training_doordash_2
)

# Constants to "hold fixed."
busy_const  <- median(training_doordash_2$total_busy_dashers, na.rm = TRUE)
onshift_const <- median(training_doordash_2$total_onshift_dashers, na.rm = TRUE)

# 2) Prediction grid: vary on-shift, hold busy fixed.
grid_onshift <- tibble(
  total_onshift_dashers = seq(
    min(training_doordash_2$total_onshift_dashers,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    max(training_doordash_2$total_onshift_dashers,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    length.out = 200
  ),
  total_busy_dashers = busy_const
) |>
  mutate(
    q10 = predict(qr10, newdata = cur_data()),
    q50 = predict(qr50, newdata = cur_data()),
    q90 = predict(qr90, newdata = cur_data())
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(q10, q50, q90), names_to = "quantile", values_to = "pred") |>
  mutate(quantile = recode(quantile, q10 = "0.1", q50 = "0.5", q90 = "0.9"))

# 3) Prediction grid: vary busy, hold on-shift fixed.
grid_busy <- tibble(
  total_busy_dashers = seq(min(training_doordash_2$total_busy_dashers, na.rm = TRUE),
    max(training_doordash_2$total_busy_dashers, na.rm = TRUE),
    length.out = 200
  ),
  total_onshift_dashers = onshift_const
) |>
  mutate(
    q10 = predict(qr10, newdata = cur_data()),
    q50 = predict(qr50, newdata = cur_data()),
    q90 = predict(qr90, newdata = cur_data())
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(q10, q50, q90), names_to = "quantile", values_to = "pred") |>
  mutate(quantile = recode(quantile, q10 = "0.1", q50 = "0.5", q90 = "0.9"))

# Plot: vary on-shift, busy held constant.
second_plot_delivery_time_vs_onshift <- ggplot(
  training_doordash_2,
  aes(x = total_onshift_dashers, y = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_onshift,
    aes(y = pred, colour = quantile),
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Total On-shift Dashers",
    y = "Actual Delivery Time (min)",
    title = "Conditional Quantile Lines (0.1, 0.5, and 0.9-quantiles) 
    versus Total On-shift Dashers",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Holding total busy dashers constant at its median of ",
      round(busy_const, 1), " dashers"
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 22),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 22),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 21, margin = margin(r = 1, unit = "cm")),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold")
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Quantile", reverse = TRUE))

# Plot: vary busy, on-shift held constant.
second_plot_delivery_time_vs_busy <- ggplot(
  training_doordash_2,
  aes(x = total_busy_dashers, y = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_busy,
    aes(y = pred, colour = quantile),
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Total Busy Dashers",
    y = "Actual Delivery Time (min)",
    title = "Conditional Quantile Lines (0.1, 0.5, and 0.9-quantiles) 
    versus Total Busy Dashers",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Holding total onshift dashers constant at its median of ",
      round(onshift_const, 1),
      " dashers"
    )
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 24, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 22),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 22),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 21, margin = margin(r = 1, unit = "cm")),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold")
  ) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(title = "Quantile", reverse = TRUE))

second_plot_delivery_time_vs_onshift
second_plot_delivery_time_vs_busy
```

Now, let us deliver a suitable plot for `store_primary_category` versus `actual_delivery_time`.

## Third Statistical Inquiry: Build a conservative ETA range for a specific order (probabilistic prediction) {.unnumbered}

Let us go back to the Chipotle screenshot (see below) to get the corresponding context:

![Screenshot from Alexi's phone.](img/doordash.png){width=45%}

Now, your manager says:

> “*We also need an actual ETA range for a specific order via Quantile regression, such as the one from the Chipotle screenshot. And I want it conservative so we don’t underestimate late deliveries.*”

Here, we focus on **prediction** and its **probabilistic interpretation**. That said, instead of focusing on parametric modelling, let us switch to the non-parametric counterpart to capture local behaviours in our regressors with greater predictive accuracy.

::: {.callout-important}
## Important

**Why should we use $\tau = 0.1$ and $\tau = 0.9$?**

Because DoorDash would want an interval that roughly captures the middle 80% of outcomes. Suppose we have $k$ regressors in our Quantile regression model:

$$
P\left[\widehat{Q}_{Y|X_1, \dots, X_k}(\tau = 0.1 \mid X_1, \dots, X_k) \le Y \le \widehat{Q}_{Y|X_1, \dots, X_k}(\tau = 0.9 \mid X_1, \dots, X_k)\right] \approx 0.8.
$$

Using the word **probability** is valid here because quantiles correspond to probabilistic statements about the conditional distribution.
:::

## Q1.12.  Exploratory Data Analysis with Estimated Non-parametric Quantile Regressions ($\tau = 0.1, 0.9$) {.unnumbered}

This inquiry will involve EDA and estimation, all combined, since we need to both estimate and visualize our modelling approaches for predictions. We will use `rqss()` with smooth terms `qss()` (i.e., quantile smoothing splines). 

> **Choosing the smoothing strength $\lambda$:** Here we pick $\lambda$ using visual inspection (a practical "*sanity check*" to avoid obvious under/overfitting). In a more formal workflow, we can tune $\lambda$ via $K$-fold cross-validation by minimizing [the pinball loss](https://pages.github.ubc.ca/mds-2025-26/DSCI_562_regr-2_students/notes/lecture7_quantile_regression.html#eq-fidelity-function) (a.k.a. the fidelity function we saw in class), which measures how well the model predicts the target conditional quantile.

> **Smoothing tip:**
>
> - Smaller `lambda` = wigglier fitted curve (risk overfit).
>
> - Larger `lambda` = smoother fitted curve (risk underfit).
>
> We want a “*Goldilocks*” fit (i.e., a regression model that is flexible enough to capture the true pattern in the data while balancing bias and variance).

Before visualizing the non-parametric fitted curves for the $0.1$ and $0.9$-quantiles, we need to fit our two non-parametric Quantile regressions for `actual_delivery_time` versus `total_onshift_dashers`, `total_busy_dashers`, `store_primary_category`. **Note that we cannot use `qss()` on `store_primary_category` given it is a categorical regressor, and this function is only meant for numerical regressors.** 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# Choose a moderate smoothing strength (you can adjust after visual inspection)
lambda_choice <- 10

qrss_10 <- rqss(
  actual_delivery_time ~
    qss(total_onshift_dashers, lambda = lambda_choice) +
    qss(total_busy_dashers, lambda = lambda_choice) + store_primary_category,
  tau = 0.10,
  data = training_doordash_2
)

qrss_90 <- rqss(
  actual_delivery_time ~
    qss(total_onshift_dashers, lambda = lambda_choice) +
    qss(total_busy_dashers, lambda = lambda_choice) + store_primary_category,
  tau = 0.90,
  data = training_doordash_2
)
```

Then, we will visualize the non-parametric quantile fits of `actual_delivery_time` versus `total_onshift_dashers` and `total_busy_dashers` (*we vary one regressor and hold others fixed*).

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 9
# Hold these regressors at typical values for plotting
fixed_busy <- median(training_doordash_2$total_busy_dashers)
fixed_onshift <- median(training_doordash_2$total_onshift_dashers)

# On-shift dashers plot grid
# Let us put mexican in store_primary_category since that is
# the ETA predictive band we are aiming for (the Chipotle screenshot!)
grid_onshift_np <- tibble(
  total_onshift_dashers = seq(
    min(training_doordash_2$total_onshift_dashers),
    max(training_doordash_2$total_onshift_dashers),
    length.out = 200
  ),
  total_busy_dashers = fixed_busy,
  store_primary_category = "mexican"
) |>
  mutate(
    store_primary_category = factor(store_primary_category,
      levels = levels(training_doordash_2$store_primary_category)
    ),
    pred_q10 = predict(qrss_10, newdata = cur_data()),
    pred_q90 = predict(qrss_90, newdata = cur_data())
  )

# Actual delivery versus on-shift dashers 
# while keeping cuisine at Mexican and busy dashers at its median
third_plot_delivery_time_vs_onshift <- ggplot(
  training_doordash_2,
  aes(x = total_onshift_dashers, y = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_onshift_np,
    aes(y = pred_q10, colour = "0.1"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_onshift_np,
    aes(y = pred_q90, colour = "0.9"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "Quantile",
    values = c("0.1" = "red", "0.9" = "blue"),
    breaks = c("0.9", "0.1")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Total On-shift Dashers",
    y = "Actual Delivery time (min)",
    title = "Non-parametric quantile curves (0.1 and 0.9-quantiles)",
    subtitle = "Total busy dashers and cuisine type held constant (median and Mexican,
    respectively)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 23, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 22),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 21, margin = margin(r = 1, unit = "cm")),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold")
  )

# Busy dashers plot grid
# Let us put mexican in store_primary_category since that is
# the ETA predictive band we are aiming for (the Chipotle screenshot!)
grid_busy_np <- tibble(
  total_busy_dashers = seq(
    min(training_doordash_2$total_busy_dashers),
    max(training_doordash_2$total_busy_dashers),
    length.out = 200
  ),
  total_onshift_dashers = fixed_onshift,
  store_primary_category = "mexican"
) |>
  mutate(
    store_primary_category = factor(store_primary_category,
      levels = levels(training_doordash_2$store_primary_category)
    ),
    pred_q10 = predict(qrss_10, newdata = cur_data()),
    pred_q90 = predict(qrss_90, newdata = cur_data())
  )

# Actual delivery versus busy dashers 
# while keeping cuisine at Mexican and on-shift dashers at its median
third_plot_delivery_time_vs_busy <- ggplot(
  training_doordash_2,
  aes(x = total_busy_dashers, y = actual_delivery_time)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_busy_np,
    aes(y = pred_q10, colour = "0.1"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = grid_busy_np,
    aes(y = pred_q90, colour = "0.9"),
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    name = "Quantile",
    values = c("0.1" = "red", "0.9" = "blue"),
    breaks = c("0.9", "0.1")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Total Busy Dashers",
    y = "Actual Delivery time (min)",
    title = "Non-parametric quantile curves (0.1 and 0.9-quantiles)",
    subtitle = "Total on-shift dashers and cuisine type held constant (median and Mexican, 
    respectively)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 23, face = "bold"),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 17),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 22),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 21, margin = margin(r = 1, unit = "cm")),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 21, face = "bold")
  )

third_plot_delivery_time_vs_onshift
third_plot_delivery_time_vs_busy
```
